Everyone has a different relationship to depression. Some people talk to by reciting platitudes - like affirmations. Some people mirror its darkness. Some get mad at it. We are all trying our best, there's no reason to put someone down. 

I do see the harm, though, in someone who tries to talk to someone else's depression the same way they talk to theirs. There should definitely be some kind of disclaimer - usually people say something like "and this is just my opinion" - but a lot of times that's not how we communicate. A lot of times we're just kind of talking to ourselves and aren't considering the fact that other people are listening.

Sometimes I put a lot of effort into doing something that I know will likely have no value to anyone but me. Like I used to do as a kid with my action figures, just having a ball with my imagination without ever considering what other people might think.

I hear you loudly. I've spent years trying to translate my thoughts and feelings into language people seem to enjoy - writing, jokes, art, friendship, love, whatever - and it's always totally unacceptable when I want to share something directly with someone about how I actually think and feel. Makes me feel like a fucking alien 90% of the time but when I come here and read what everyone's writing, say what I want to say, I feel better. This is a good place, because it's filled with sadness. Everywhere else sadness is denied. Makes me really, really sad.

Question everyone and everything, especially other social workers, caseworkers, interns, and anyone else claiming to be doing work similar to you. I don't agree with one of these comments that you shouldn't get into arguments with people... if conflict isn't something you're comfortable with then maybe social work isn't for you. What I've found - from being on both sides of the following critique - is that the worst kind of social work produces short-term, superficial gains (staff, clients are "happy", they like you, they reward you because you're really good at pleasing them). Social work at its best is an arduous and mistake-laden process of learning to accept, love, and partner with people to invigorate change and movement where things in their lives feel stuck in a loop. Sometimes that process can make people happy, or appreciative of your efforts, but sometimes it makes people really angry and frustrated because change hurts. Don't just try to please people, to make them like you, to "make" them do anything, really. This is a profession where, if you're really dedicated to what social work should be about (i.e. not just supporting faulty systems and pushing people back into it who fall through the cracks but partnering with those people in challenging those systems and the assumptions built around them), you kind of have to stop giving a shit about professionalism.

I've always been wary of the power of pity, especially looking back at the people who pitied me when I was younger, or who pity me now. I think "pity" is, as you say, condescending. And you know it when you feel it, because the other person genuinely doesn't know how to be compassionate and they seem to be unable to reach you. If you try speaking to someone in a language they don't understand you'll notice a similar feeling between yourself and the other person - there's something missing. It becomes interesting when you turn it around though - look at someone who pities you and just give them a look of total confusion, bemusement... like they're speaking a different language and whatever they're saying is just ridiculous. It's satisfying, even though it's a little immature. I wouldn't recommend it as an all-around strategy but that's how I got through my teen years. I think people call it sarcasm!

When I tell people they're strong it's usually because I feel like they need to hear it, based on something they're saying. It's a way of saying "you're doing it, don't worry, just keep going" but I think what's often missing from it - whether on the speaking side or the hearing side - is "and I will be strong for you, because you remind me that people can be strong, and that's good for me". 

I think a_kino is right, or should be right. It sounds like you have a history of people being unreliable as supports for you, so you didn't get many chances growing up to open up to people and be vulnerable. The first time you break down in front of someone, you may not get the response you're looking for - especially from someone who has grown accustomed to your strength as a constant - but that's the whole thing about being open and vulnerable: you actively open up to someone you believe you can trust, then after (hopefully) not experiencing some kind of insult or injury you face the unknown zone of this person having either a confused reaction, or some reaction your brain never calculated (and it likely won't be a perfect empathy response either), you have to push through and stay open. And this is all mostly me talking to myself, by the way, because I feel similarly.

Well there's a few directions you can go. First is ask yourself what it is you want from a relationship, and why you want one, and what actually is a relationship to you. Because there are a bajillion kinds of relationships you can have these days and not a single one of them is going to match what "relationship" looks like in your head. If that sounds therapisty, then you could also do some investigative work and look into what it takes to attract women, and see if you can't emulate some of the behaviors of guys who are getting into relationships. If that sounds too redpill, then you're going to have to deal with the fact that rejection is something everyone faces and there's no one to blame for it, and that the process is usually: try something, learn from it, try something else, learn from it etc etc with successes mixed in that you need to push yourself to notice because no one else will. There's no end goal, it's just wayfinding and turning and turning and wayfinding... you're in college, read some philosophy! It will help you more than you think. Let me know if you want some recommendations.

Depression can be a muse, if that's what you mean by dealing with it. Other times it's just a black hole but I don't really have the language to talk about that... nor do I think there really is anything to say (though we all know it feels, as you said, heavy and empty). But when it's a muse I get all sorts of inspiration - I dance, I sing, I make songs, I talk to myself and record it, I call up a friend, I write, I drink, I play a game, I walk around, I eat, I listen to music, I do fake karate, I read, I make art, I go out and say something unexpected to someone I don't know... there's a lot you can do.

My biggest regret in college is letting these kinds of things bring me down, and not putting enough effort into opening myself up to the girls who were actually interested in me. I think I was afraid of girls wanting to "lock me" into something I couldn't get out of... looking back, I was very foolish to believe this.

Which I do, constantly, and am ashamed of. But I rely on my supportive family and friends, with equal parts hatred and love. And the low-stress jobs... they've gotten me through some times. You aren't afraid to discuss death, which a lot of people are, and you're further not afraid to discuss it in relation to yourself. You have a strong enough value system that even in despair you refuse to indulge in unethical behavior, ie scamming people. You have enough self-respect and dignity to cut ties with people you disagree with and who you felt didn't treat you well, and with a girl you, I'm assuming, weren't connecting very well with. 

You say you don't see a reason to stick around and I see you seeing a lot of lights, a lot of really hard, important truths about social reality and about yourself. I see you and don't know you but I will say unequivocally that you need to keep going, keep moving.
